Actus is the agent orchestration layer of the SSCCS stack, licensed under
Apache-2.0. It plans with the LLM, holds conversation state and workspace
context, and commands the execution agents that convert plans into system
effects. The default execution agent is Telos, the general headless agent
layer of the stack. Telos runs as a separate native process and speaks an
ACP-over-WebSocket contract; actus never links or bundles agent code, so
the Apache-2.0 actus image carries no GPL-3.0-or-later Telos code.

The orchestration surface is agent-agnostic. Every agent kind implements
one `AgentBackend` trait, and an `AgentRegistry` maps names to running
adapters. Telos is the default kind. A native in-process adapter serves
as a reference and for tests, and further kinds plug in behind the same
surface. Configuration lives in `~/.actus/config.toml`: each `[[agents]]`
entry sets kind, provider, model, binary path, WebSocket port, tool
approval policy, and the MCP servers injected into the agent. Without a
config file, actus derives a single default Telos agent from CLI flags
and environment variables.

A large language model by itself is stateless. Every interaction starts
from zero. The infrastructure around it must manage conversation history,
provide context about the workspace, and command a tool-carrying
executor. Actus provides the orchestration: it owns threads and context,
and drives Telos as its instrument for file edits, command runs, and
network effects. The client sees one headless service with no GUI, no
display server, and no browser.

The shape mirrors the layer below. neXus realizes its purpose through
chton, the single low-level executor over the coordinate space. Actus
does the same with Telos: the orchestra decides, the executor acts, and
the agent underneath stays replaceable behind the contract.

## Architecture

The architecture follows a layered separation of concerns:

- **HTTP API Layer**: Exposes the agent's capabilities over REST with streaming support for real-time response delivery, guarded by bearer-token authentication. Clients interact through a uniform interface without needing to manage the agent process directly.

- **Session State and Persistence**: Manages conversation threads per agent across reconnections. Each thread maintains its full message history under `~/.actus/threads/{agent}`, so the agent resumes from where it left off even after connection drops or server restarts.

- **Agent Registry and Bridge**: The communication channel between the server and the agent processes. The Telos adapter speaks ACP over WebSocket and handles automatic reconnection, message delivery guarantees, and the lifecycle of the agent process. Each configured agent carries its own tool approval policy (`always`, `ask`, `never`) and its injected MCP servers, and the policy is carried to the agent on launch.

- **Workspace Context**: Provides filesystem-level and git-aware context to the agent. Enables file search, symbol search, project rule discovery, repository structure awareness, and workspace navigation. Context mentions can pull file contents, symbol definitions, rule files, and public URLs behind an SSRF guard.

## Design Principles

**Stateless client, stateful server.** Clients send individual messages without managing conversation history. The server tracks thread state, injects prior context, and presents a coherent narrative to the agent on each turn.

**Headless by default.** The agent runs without any graphical interface. This eliminates the dependency on desktop environments, display servers, and browser runtimes, making the system deployable on servers, containers, edge nodes, and embedded devices.

**Protocol isolation.** The server owns the agent lifecycle and communication protocol. Clients interact only through HTTP, insulating them from changes in the underlying agent protocol or implementation.

**Thin runtime with process-separated agents.** The runtime links no agent implementation. Agents are external processes located by path and reached over a contract, so the Apache-2.0 actus image never carries GPL Telos code, and an agent can be swapped without changing the server. The published runtime image holds only the actus binary and git.

## Status and Direction

Actus is Apache-2.0 licensed, pre-release, and in active development. The
actus to Telos contract works end to end: Telos connects over WebSocket
and serves threads, tools, and cancellation. Deterministic conformance
tests run without an LLM in CI, using a stub agent for the mock-only
tier and a fake backend for the contract scenarios, beside the live local
suite. Per-agent thread persistence, bearer-token authentication,
per-agent tool approval, and MCP injection are in place.

Packaging follows the thin runtime: a multi-stage Dockerfile builds a
test image for CI and a slim runtime image for publishing. The Rust unit
and integration suites run on the test image, and published images are
cut on version tags (a versioned image plus `latest`) or as manual dev
snapshots, so ordinary development commits publish nothing.

Current direction:

- **Multi-agent operation.** Keep Telos as the professional execution
  core and add lightweight auxiliary agents behind the same registry, the
  first trial of a one-plus-a deployment. The first candidate is Ante, a
  single-binary terminal agent whose source is Apache-2.0 and whose
  prebuilt binary ships under separate preview terms; actus would drive
  it through its JSONL serve protocol or headless one-shot mode.
- **neXus integration.** Archive long-running conversations on the neXus
  blackboard and accumulate knowledge across sessions.
- **Wider tool coverage through Telos.** Extend the endpoint surface that
  the orchestration layer exposes without coupling to a single agent
  implementation.
